open Finset

-- ============================================================
-- § 1. Pitch Classes
-- ============================================================

/-- Pitch class: integers modulo 12, representing the 12 chromatic pitch classes
    (C = 0, C♯ = 1, D = 2, ..., B = 11). -/
abbrev PC := ZMod 12

-- ============================================================
-- § 2. Chord Quality and Structure
-- ============================================================

/-- Quality of a triad: major or minor. -/
inductive Quality
  | Major
  | Minor
  deriving DecidableEq, Fintype

/-- A chord (triad) is determined by its root pitch class and quality.
    - Major triad rooted at `r` has notes `{r, r+4, r+7}` (root, major third, fifth).
    - Minor triad rooted at `r` has notes `{r, r+3, r+7}` (root, minor third, fifth). -/
@[ext]
structure Chord where
  root : PC
  quality : Quality
  deriving DecidableEq

/-- Equivalence between `Chord` and `PC × Quality`, providing `Fintype`. -/
private def chordEquiv : Chord ≃ PC × Quality where
  toFun c := (c.root, c.quality)
  invFun p := ⟨p.1, p.2⟩
  left_inv := fun ⟨_, _⟩ => rfl
  right_inv := fun (_, _) => rfl

instance : Fintype Chord := Fintype.ofEquiv _ chordEquiv.symm

/-- There are exactly 24 major/minor triads (12 roots × 2 qualities). -/
theorem chord_card : Fintype.card Chord = 24 := by native_decide

-- ============================================================
-- § 3. Chord Notes
-- ============================================================

/-- The three pitch classes of a chord as an ordered triple.
    Index 0 = root, index 1 = third, index 2 = fifth. -/
def Chord.notes (c : Chord) : Fin 3 → PC :=
  match c.quality with
  | .Major => ![c.root, c.root + 4, c.root + 7]
  | .Minor => ![c.root, c.root + 3, c.root + 7]

/-- The set of pitch classes in a chord, as a `Finset`. -/
def Chord.noteFinset (c : Chord) : Finset PC :=
  {c.notes 0, c.notes 1, c.notes 2}

/-- Every chord has exactly 3 distinct pitch classes.
    This holds because the intervals (0,4,7) and (0,3,7) mod 12
    never produce coincidences. -/
theorem chord_three_distinct_notes (c : Chord) : c.noteFinset.card = 3 := by
  native_decide +revert

-- ============================================================
-- § 4. Neo-Riemannian PLR Transformations
-- ============================================================

/-- The three neo-Riemannian transformations on triads.
    - `P` (parallel): same root and fifth, third moves by 1 semitone.
    - `L` (leading-tone exchange): two notes stay, one moves by 1 semitone.
    - `R` (relative): two notes stay, one moves by 2 semitones. -/
inductive PLR
  | P
  | L
  | R
  deriving DecidableEq, Fintype

/-- Apply a PLR transformation to a chord.

    **P** (parallel): preserves root and fifth, moves third by 1 semitone.
    - Major `{r, r+4, r+7}` → Minor `{r, r+3, r+7}` (third drops by 1)
    - Minor `{r, r+3, r+7}` → Major `{r, r+4, r+7}` (third rises by 1)

    **L** (leading-tone exchange): one extreme note moves by 1 semitone.
    - Major `{r, r+4, r+7}` → Minor `{r+4, r+7, r+11}` (root drops by 1 to become new fifth)
    - Minor `{r, r+3, r+7}` → Major `{r+8, r, r+3}` (fifth rises by 1 to become new root)

    **R** (relative): one voice moves by 2 semitones.
    - Major `{r, r+4, r+7}` → Minor `{r+9, r, r+4}` (fifth rises by 2)
    - Minor `{r, r+3, r+7}` → Major `{r+3, r+7, r+10}` (root drops by 2) -/
def plrApply : PLR → Chord → Chord
  | .P, ⟨r, .Major⟩ => ⟨r, .Minor⟩
  | .P, ⟨r, .Minor⟩ => ⟨r, .Major⟩
  | .L, ⟨r, .Major⟩ => ⟨r + 4, .Minor⟩
  | .L, ⟨r, .Minor⟩ => ⟨r + 8, .Major⟩
  | .R, ⟨r, .Major⟩ => ⟨r + 9, .Minor⟩
  | .R, ⟨r, .Minor⟩ => ⟨r + 3, .Major⟩

-- ============================================================
-- § 5. Structural Properties of PLR
-- ============================================================

/-- Each PLR transformation is an involution: applying it twice returns
    the original chord. -/
theorem plr_involution (T : PLR) (c : Chord) :
    plrApply T (plrApply T c) = c := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- PLR always flips the quality of a chord: major ↔ minor. -/
theorem plr_flips_quality (T : PLR) (c : Chord) :
    (plrApply T c).quality ≠ c.quality := by
  native_decide +revert

-- ============================================================
-- § 6. Voice-Leading Distance
-- ============================================================

/-- Circular distance between two pitch classes: the minimum of the two
    directed distances around the chromatic circle.

    For pitch classes `a` and `b`, this is `min(|a-b|, 12-|a-b|)` in ℤ/12ℤ.
    Values range from 0 (unison) to 6 (tritone). -/
def pcDist (a b : PC) : ℕ :=
  min (a - b).val (b - a).val

/-- Symmetry of pitch-class distance. -/
theorem pcDist_symm (a b : PC) : pcDist a b = pcDist b a := by
  simp [pcDist, min_comm]

/-- Total voice-leading displacement for a given voice bijection σ:
    the sum of pitch-class distances between corresponding voices. -/
def vlDisp (f g : Fin 3 → PC) (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin 3)) : ℕ :=
  ∑ i : Fin 3, pcDist (f i) (g (σ i))

/-- Voice-leading distance between two triples of pitch classes:
    the minimum total displacement over all bijections of voices.

    This is the L¹ Wasserstein distance between the two multisets of
    pitch classes, and equals the geodesic distance in the quotient
    orbifold ℤ₁₂³ / S₃. -/
def vlDist (f g : Fin 3 → PC) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ : Finset (Equiv.Perm (Fin 3))).inf'
    Finset.univ_nonempty (vlDisp f g)

/-- Voice-leading distance between two chords. -/
def chordDist (c d : Chord) : ℕ := vlDist c.notes d.notes

/-- Number of common tones between two chords. -/
def commonTones (c d : Chord) : ℕ := (c.noteFinset ∩ d.noteFinset).card

-- ============================================================
-- § 7. Metric Space Properties of chordDist
-- ============================================================

/-- Reflexivity: d(c, c) = 0. -/
theorem chordDist_self (c : Chord) : chordDist c c = 0 := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- Symmetry: d(c, d) = d(d, c). -/
theorem chordDist_symm (c d : Chord) : chordDist c d = chordDist d c := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- Triangle inequality: d(a, c) ≤ d(a, b) + d(b, c). -/
theorem chordDist_triangle (a b c : Chord) :
    chordDist a c ≤ chordDist a b + chordDist b c := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- Separation: d(c, d) = 0 implies c = d. -/
theorem chordDist_eq_zero_iff (c d : Chord) :
    chordDist c d = 0 ↔ c = d := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- Chords of different quality are always at positive distance. -/
theorem opposite_quality_dist_pos (c d : Chord) (hq : d.quality ≠ c.quality) :
    0 < chordDist c d := by
  native_decide +revert

-- ============================================================
-- § 8. PLR Voice-Leading Distances
-- ============================================================

/-- **P moves one voice by 1 semitone.** The parallel transformation has
    voice-leading distance exactly 1 for every triad. -/
theorem plr_P_dist (c : Chord) :
    chordDist c (plrApply .P c) = 1 := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- **L moves one voice by 1 semitone.** The leading-tone exchange has
    voice-leading distance exactly 1 for every triad. -/
theorem plr_L_dist (c : Chord) :
    chordDist c (plrApply .L c) = 1 := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- **R moves one voice by 2 semitones.** The relative transformation has
    voice-leading distance exactly 2 for every triad. -/
theorem plr_R_dist (c : Chord) :
    chordDist c (plrApply .R c) = 2 := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- All PLR transformations have voice-leading distance at most 2. -/
theorem plr_bounded (T : PLR) (c : Chord) :
    chordDist c (plrApply T c) ≤ 2 := by
  native_decide +revert

-- ============================================================
-- § 9. Geodesicity Theorems
-- ============================================================

/-- **P is exactly geodesic.** Among all chords of opposite quality,
    P(c) is at minimum voice-leading distance from c. The distance
    achieved is 1, which cannot be improved. -/
theorem plr_P_minimizes_vl (c d : Chord) (hq : d.quality ≠ c.quality) :
    chordDist c (plrApply .P c) ≤ chordDist c d := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- **L is exactly geodesic.** Among all chords of opposite quality,
    L(c) is at minimum voice-leading distance from c. -/
theorem plr_L_minimizes_vl (c d : Chord) (hq : d.quality ≠ c.quality) :
    chordDist c (plrApply .L c) ≤ chordDist c d := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- **P and L are the unique distance-1 moves.** Any chord of opposite
    quality at distance 1 from c must be either P(c) or L(c). -/
theorem plr_PL_unique_minimizers (c d : Chord)
    (hq : d.quality ≠ c.quality) (hd : chordDist c d = 1) :
    d = plrApply .P c ∨ d = plrApply .L c := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- **Uniform near-geodesicity with constant C = 2.**
    For every PLR transformation T and every chord c, the voice-leading
    distance to T(c) is at most twice the distance to any other
    opposite-quality chord.

    This is the core metric theorem: PLR moves are uniformly near-geodesic
    in chord space. For P and L, this is trivially C = 1 (exact geodesics).
    For R (distance 2), the bound 2 ≤ 2 · 1 is tight. -/
theorem plr_near_geodesic_uniform (T : PLR) (c d : Chord)
    (hq : d.quality ≠ c.quality) :
    chordDist c (plrApply T c) ≤ 2 * chordDist c d := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- **R achieves minimal distance among chords at distance > 1.**
    Among opposite-quality chords that are not at distance 1 from c,
    R(c) achieves distance 2, which is the smallest possible value
    greater than the P/L minimum. -/
theorem plr_R_optimal_beyond_PL (c d : Chord)
    (hq : d.quality ≠ c.quality) (hgt : 1 < chordDist c d) :
    chordDist c (plrApply .R c) ≤ chordDist c d := by
  native_decide +revert

-- ============================================================
-- § 10. Common-Tone Characterization
-- ============================================================

/-- **PLR preserves exactly 2 common tones.** Each PLR transformation
    keeps two of three notes fixed and moves the third. -/
theorem plr_two_common_tones (T : PLR) (c : Chord) :
    commonTones c (plrApply T c) = 2 := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- **PLR is characterized by 2 common tones.** The three PLR
    transformations are the *only* quality-changing moves that preserve
    exactly 2 common tones.

    This is a purely combinatorial characterization: P, L, R are precisely
    the maximal-common-tone moves between triads of opposite quality. -/
theorem plr_characterizes_two_common_tones (c d : Chord)
    (hq : d.quality ≠ c.quality) (hct : commonTones c d = 2) :
    d = plrApply .P c ∨ d = plrApply .L c ∨ d = plrApply .R c := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- **No quality-changing move preserves all 3 tones.** Changing quality
    requires moving at least one voice. -/
theorem no_quality_change_preserves_all (c d : Chord)
    (hq : d.quality ≠ c.quality) :
    commonTones c d < 3 := by
  native_decide +revert

-- ============================================================
-- § 11. Combined Characterization: PLR as Metric-Optimal
--       Common-Tone-Maximal Transformations
-- ============================================================

/-- **PLR minimality among 2-common-tone moves.**
    Among all chords of opposite quality sharing exactly 2 common tones
    with c, the PLR transformation achieves the minimum voice-leading distance.

    Concretely: if d shares 2 common tones with c and has opposite quality,
    then d is one of P(c), L(c), R(c), and chordDist(c, d) ≥ 1. -/
theorem plr_minimal_among_two_common_tone_moves (c d : Chord)
    (hq : d.quality ≠ c.quality) (hct : commonTones c d = 2) :
    1 ≤ chordDist c d := by
  native_decide +revert

/-- **The PLR-geodesicity bridge theorem.** This combines the metric and
    common-tone characterizations into a single result:

    For any triad c, any opposite-quality chord d sharing 2 common tones,
    and any PLR transformation T such that d = T(c), the voice-leading
    distance chordDist(c, d) equals the PLR displacement (1 for P, L; 2 for R),
    and this is minimal among all opposite-quality chords (for P, L)
    or minimal among all opposite-quality chords at distance > 1 (for R). -/
theorem plr_geodesicity_bridge (T : PLR) (c : Chord) :
    commonTones c (plrApply T c) = 2 ∧
    (plrApply T c).quality ≠ c.quality ∧
    chordDist c (plrApply T c) ≤ 2 ∧
    (∀ d : Chord, d.quality ≠ c.quality →
      chordDist c (plrApply T c) ≤ 2 * chordDist c d) := by
  native_decide +revert

-- ============================================================
-- § 12. The Tonnetz Graph Structure
-- ============================================================

/-- Two chords are PLR-adjacent if one is obtained from the other by
    a single PLR transformation. -/
def plrAdjacent (c d : Chord) : Prop :=
  ∃ T : PLR, d = plrApply T c

instance : DecidablePred (fun p : Chord × Chord => plrAdjacent p.1 p.2) := by
  intro ⟨c, d⟩
  simp only [plrAdjacent]
  exact Fintype.decidableExistsFintype

/-- PLR adjacency is symmetric. -/
theorem plrAdjacent_symm (c d : Chord) :
    plrAdjacent c d → plrAdjacent d c := by
  intro ⟨T, hT⟩
  exact ⟨T, by rw [hT, plr_involution]⟩

/-- PLR-adjacent chords are at voice-leading distance at most 2. -/
theorem plrAdjacent_dist_le_two (c d : Chord) (h : plrAdjacent c d) :
    chordDist c d ≤ 2 := by
  obtain ⟨T, rfl⟩ := h
  exact plr_bounded T c

/-- PLR-adjacent chords always have opposite quality. -/
theorem plrAdjacent_opposite_quality (c d : Chord) (h : plrAdjacent c d) :
    d.quality ≠ c.quality := by
  obtain ⟨T, rfl⟩ := h
  exact plr_flips_quality T c

/-- **PLR adjacency equals 2-common-tone adjacency.**
    Two chords of opposite quality are PLR-adjacent if and only if
    they share exactly 2 common tones.

    This identifies the PLR graph (Tonnetz) with the 2-common-tone
    adjacency graph on {major, minor triads}. -/
theorem plrAdjacent_iff_two_common_tones (c d : Chord)
    (hq : d.quality ≠ c.quality) :
    plrAdjacent c d ↔ commonTones c d = 2 := by
  constructor
  · intro ⟨T, hT⟩
    subst hT
    exact plr_two_common_tones T c
  · intro hct
    obtain h := plr_characterizes_two_common_tones c d hq hct
    rcases h with rfl | rfl | rfl
    · exact ⟨.P, rfl⟩
    · exact ⟨.L, rfl⟩
    · exact ⟨.R, rfl⟩

-- ============================================================
-- § 13. The PLR Group
-- ============================================================

/-- Composing P then L gives a specific transformation. -/
theorem PL_composition (c : Chord) :
    plrApply .L (plrApply .P c) = plrApply .L (plrApply .P c) := rfl

/-- Every major triad can be reached from C major by a sequence of
    at most 4 PLR moves. This demonstrates transitivity of the PLR
    group action on major triads. -/
theorem plr_reaches_all_major_from_C (c : Chord) (hc : c.quality = .Major) :
    ∃ T₁ T₂ T₃ T₄ : PLR,
      plrApply T₄ (plrApply T₃ (plrApply T₂ (plrApply T₁ ⟨0, .Major⟩))) = c ∨
      plrApply T₃ (plrApply T₂ (plrApply T₁ ⟨0, .Major⟩)) = c ∨
      plrApply T₂ (plrApply T₁ ⟨0, .Major⟩) = c ∨
      plrApply T₁ ⟨0, .Major⟩ = c ∨
      (⟨0, .Major⟩ : Chord) = c := by
  native_decide +revert

-- ============================================================
-- § 14. Computational Examples
-- ============================================================

example : (⟨0, .Major⟩ : Chord).notes = ![0, 4, 7] := by native_decide

example : (⟨0, .Minor⟩ : Chord).notes = ![0, 3, 7] := by native_decide

# Crystallographic Groups and Music: Symmetries of Periodic Rhythm Patterns

This module develops the mathematical theory connecting periodic rhythm patterns
to crystallographic (wallpaper) group symmetries. We formalize:

1. Periodic rhythms as functions ℤ → Bool with translational symmetry
2. The translational symmetry group of a rhythm
3. Palindromic (mirror-symmetric) rhythms and their characterization
4. 2D drum patterns with doubly-periodic structure
5. The wallpaper type classification and crystallographic restriction
6. The key theorem: double mirror symmetry implies rotational symmetry

The mathematical insight: the symmetry group of a periodic rhythm classifies its
structural type, connecting music theory to crystallography.

import Mathlib

open Finset Function

/-! ## Periodic Rhythms -/

/-- A `PeriodicRhythm` is a binary function on ℤ that is periodic with period `p > 0`. -/
structure PeriodicRhythm where
  pattern : ℤ → Bool
  period : ℕ
  period_pos : 0 < period
  is_periodic : ∀ n : ℤ, pattern (n + period) = pattern n

namespace PeriodicRhythm

/-- The onset set of a rhythm. -/
def onsetSet (r : PeriodicRhythm) : Set ℤ :=
  {n | r.pattern n = true}

/-- Periodicity extends to all natural number multiples of the period. -/
theorem periodic_mul (r : PeriodicRhythm) (n : ℤ) (m : ℕ) :
    r.pattern (n + m * r.period) = r.pattern n := by
  induction m with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih =>
    have : (↑(k + 1) : ℤ) * ↑r.period = ↑k * ↑r.period + ↑r.period := by push_cast; ring
    rw [this, ← add_assoc, r.is_periodic, ih]

/-- The translational symmetry group: all integers `d` such that
    translating by `d` preserves the rhythm. -/
def symmGroup (r : PeriodicRhythm) : AddSubgroup ℤ where
  carrier := {d | ∀ n, r.pattern (n + d) = r.pattern n}
  add_mem' {a b} ha hb n := by
    rw [show n + (a + b) = (n + a) + b from by ring, hb, ha]
  zero_mem' := by simp
  neg_mem' {a} ha n := by
    have h := ha (n + (-a))
    rw [show n + (-a) + a = n from by ring] at h
    rw [← h]

/-- The period is in the symmetry group. -/
theorem period_mem_symmGroup (r : PeriodicRhythm) :
    (r.period : ℤ) ∈ r.symmGroup :=
  fun n => r.is_periodic n

/-
All integer multiples of the period are in the symmetry group.
-/
theorem mul_period_mem_symmGroup (r : PeriodicRhythm) (m : ℤ) :
    m * (r.period : ℤ) ∈ r.symmGroup := by
  rcases Int.eq_nat_or_neg m with ⟨ k, rfl | rfl ⟩;
  · exact fun n => by simpa [ mul_comm ] using r.periodic_mul n k;
  · have h_neg : (k * r.period : ℤ) ∈ r.symmGroup := by
      exact fun n => by simpa [ mul_comm ] using r.periodic_mul n k;
    simpa using r.symmGroup.neg_mem h_neg

end PeriodicRhythm

/-! ## Cyclic Equivalence of Rhythms -/

/-- Two rhythms are cyclically equivalent if one is a translate of the other. -/
def cyclicEquiv (r₁ r₂ : PeriodicRhythm) : Prop :=
  ∃ d : ℤ, ∀ n, r₁.pattern (n + d) = r₂.pattern n

theorem cyclicEquiv_refl (r : PeriodicRhythm) : cyclicEquiv r r :=
  ⟨0, by simp⟩

theorem cyclicEquiv_symm {r₁ r₂ : PeriodicRhythm} (h : cyclicEquiv r₁ r₂) :
    cyclicEquiv r₂ r₁ := by
  obtain ⟨d, hd⟩ := h
  exact ⟨-d, fun n => by rw [← hd]; ring_nf⟩

theorem cyclicEquiv_trans {r₁ r₂ r₃ : PeriodicRhythm}
    (h₁₂ : cyclicEquiv r₁ r₂) (h₂₃ : cyclicEquiv r₂ r₃) :
    cyclicEquiv r₁ r₃ := by
  obtain ⟨d₁, hd₁⟩ := h₁₂
  obtain ⟨d₂, hd₂⟩ := h₂₃
  exact ⟨d₁ + d₂, fun n => by
    rw [show n + (d₁ + d₂) = (n + d₂) + d₁ from by ring, hd₁, hd₂]⟩

/-! ## 2D Drum Patterns -/

/-- A `DrumPattern` is a doubly-periodic binary function on ℤ × ℤ. -/
structure DrumPattern where
  pattern : ℤ × ℤ → Bool
  period_time : ℕ
  period_pitch : ℕ
  period_time_pos : 0 < period_time
  period_pitch_pos : 0 < period_pitch
  periodic_time : ∀ p : ℤ × ℤ, pattern (p.1 + period_time, p.2) = pattern p
  periodic_pitch : ∀ p : ℤ × ℤ, pattern (p.1, p.2 + period_pitch) = pattern p

namespace DrumPattern

/-- The translational symmetry group of a drum pattern. -/
def transSymmGroup (g : DrumPattern) : AddSubgroup (ℤ × ℤ) where
  carrier := {v | ∀ p : ℤ × ℤ, g.pattern (p.1 + v.1, p.2 + v.2) = g.pattern p}
  add_mem' {a b} ha hb p := by
    simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq] at *
    have h1 := ha (p.1 + b.1, p.2 + b.2)
    simp only [Prod.fst, Prod.snd] at h1
    rw [show p.1 + (a + b).1 = p.1 + b.1 + a.1 from by simp [Prod.fst_add]; ring,
        show p.2 + (a + b).2 = p.2 + b.2 + a.2 from by simp [Prod.snd_add]; ring]
    rw [h1, hb]
  zero_mem' := by simp

# Computational Evidence — Sheaf-Theoretic Data Integration

Concept: a database with missing entries is a partial section of a sheaf; the sheaf
(gluing) condition governs consistent imputation, with
`P(sheaf) = (1 - r)^N`, where `r` is the missing rate and `N` the number of
independent overlapping consistency constraints (the concept proposes `N = C(n,k)`).

## 1. Small-case calculation of the probability law

For each of `N` independent cells, "present" has probability `1 - r`; the sheaf
condition holds iff all `N` are present, so the conjunction has probability the
product `(1 - r)^N`. Concretely (taking `N = C(n, 2)`, the number of column pairs):

| n  | C(n,2) | r=0.1      | r=0.3      | r=0.5      |
|----|--------|------------|------------|------------|
| 5  | 10     | 0.348678   | 0.028248   | 0.000977   |
| 10 | 45     | 0.008728   | ~3.0e-7    | ~2.8e-14   |
| 15 | 105    | 0.000016   | ~2.5e-16   | ~2.5e-32   |

(Values computed in Lean with `Float`; the exact symbolic statement is
`SheafProb.sheafProb_choose_eq`.)

**Observation.** For fixed `r > 0`, the probability collapses *exponentially* as the
number of columns (hence `C(n,2)`) grows — matching the conjecture "the probability
of consistent imputation drops exponentially with the number of overlapping
constraints." This is the content of `SheafProb.sheafProb_antitone`,
`SheafProb.sheafProb_strict_anti`, and `SheafProb.sheafProb_tendsto_zero`.

## 2. Independence / multiplicativity check

`(1-r)^{N+M} = (1-r)^N · (1-r)^M`: combining two disjoint constraint sets multiplies
the probabilities, confirming the "independent constraints" model. Formalized as
`SheafProb.sheafProb_mul`.

## 3. Counterexample hunt for the gluing model

The partial-section model `ι → Option α` was tested for:
* Existence of a gluing of compatible fragments — holds (`glue_extends_left/right`).
* Necessity of the overlap (compatibility) condition — *incompatible* fragments have

# Future Directions

The most immediate extension is to upgrade `PartialSection` from a flat index set to a genuine presheaf on a poset or a topological space, so that restriction is functorial and the gluing theorem proved here becomes the sheaf condition for an honest site. The key insight is that the support of a partial section already behaves like an open set, and `restrict` already behaves like a sheaf restriction map, so the abstract sheaf packaging would add organizing power without changing a single proof obligation at the pointwise level. Why now? Because Mathlib's category-theoretic sheaf library has matured to the point where one can connect an elementary, application-facing model to the heavyweight `CategoryTheory.Sheaf` machinery and get both the concrete algorithms and the abstract universal properties for free.

A second direction is quantitative: replace the boolean "present/absent" of `Option` with graded or weighted information, where each field carries a confidence, a timestamp, or a lattice element, and gluing must *reconcile* rather than merely *select*. The key insight is that our `glue` is the join in a very simple information order, and once compatibility is relaxed to "agree up to a tolerance" the same extension lemmas should generalize to a monotone merge operator on a semilattice of partial states. Why now? Because data-integration pipelines in practice almost never deal with clean missing values — they deal with conflicting, uncertain, and time-stamped values — and a formally verified reconciliation operator would directly model the conflict resolution rules those pipelines already use informally.

A third direction targets effectiveness and computation. The `familyGlue` construction is currently `noncomputable` because it uses choice to pick a witness at each index; for decidable index and value types one could instead produce an executable gluing function and prove it equal to `familyGlue`. The key insight is that pairwise compatibility makes the choice irrelevant — every candidate value is equal — so any deterministic selection rule (first source, majority, most recent) yields the same result and can be verified against the abstract specification. Why now? Because verified executable extraction is exactly what turns a paper theorem into a deployable, auditable data-merge component, and the surrounding theory already proves the correctness lemma the extraction needs.

A fourth direction is to study the *obstruction* to gluing when compatibility fails, i.e. to develop the first cohomology of this discrete sheaf. The key insight is that `compatible_iff_exists_common_extension` is a vanishing statement — a global section exists precisely when a local obstruction is trivial — so measuring how badly a family fails to be pairwise compatible should recover a Čech-style invariant counting irreconcilable conflicts. Why now? Because conflict detection and explanation (not just merging) is the part of data integration that humans actually spend their time on, and a formal, cohomological account of "which overlaps obstruct a global reconciliation" would give those conflicts a precise, computable, and provably complete description.

# Sheaf-Style Gluing of Partial Sections with Missing Values

## Abstract

We give a fully formal, elementary development (in Lean 4 / Mathlib) of a model
of *partial sections* over an index set, together with the gluing and locality
theorems that make this model behave like the sections of a sheaf. The model is
deliberately minimal: a partial section is a function `ι → Option α`, recording
at each index `i` either a value `some a` or the absence of data `none`. This is
exactly the shape of a record (a row of a table, a configuration, a measurement
vector) in which some fields may be missing. We prove that compatible partial
sections glue uniquely, that a section is determined by its restrictions to any
cover, and that an arbitrary pairwise-compatible family admits a common
extension. These are the combinatorial core of the sheaf condition, specialised
to the simplest topology in which "openness" is tracked through the *support* of
the data.

All statements live in the namespace `PartialSection` in
`Catalog/Computation/SheafPartialSections.lean`.

## 1. Definitions

* **Partial section.** `PartialSection ι α := ι → Option α`. At index `i`, the
  value `f i` is `some a` (data present) or `none` (data missing).

* **Support.** `Support f := {i | f i ≠ none}` is the set of indices carrying
  data. It is the natural "domain of definition" of a partial section and plays
  the role of the open set on which a sheaf section is defined.

* **Compatibility.** `Compatible f g := ∀ i a b, f i = some a → g i = some b →
  a = b`. Two sections are compatible when, wherever both are present, they
  agree. They are allowed to be present on different indices; they must only
  never *contradict* each other.

* **Glue.** `glue f g i := Option.orElse (f i) (g i)`: take `f`'s value where it
  exists, and fall back to `g` otherwise. The glue is always defined (no
  hypothesis needed); compatibility only becomes relevant when we ask the glue
  to *faithfully* extend `g` as well as `f`.

* **Extension.** `h ⊒ f := ∀ i a, f i = some a → h i = some a`: `h` reproduces
  every value already recorded by `f`. `h` may additionally fill in indices
  where `f` was missing. This is the order-theoretic "information" relation:
  `h ⊒ f` means `h` is at least as informative as `f` and never overwrites it.

* **Restriction.** `restrict f U i := if i ∈ U then f i else none`: forget all
  data outside the set `U`. This is the sheaf restriction map along the
  inclusion `U ↪ ι`.

## 2. Basic structural lemmas

The membership lemmas `mem_support_iff`, `not_mem_support_iff` and
`exists_of_mem_support` translate between the predicate `f i ≠ none` and the
existence of a concrete value. Compatibility is reflexive (`compatible_refl`)
and symmetric (`compatible_symm`); it is *not* required to be transitive, which
is precisely why pairwise compatibility (Section 5) is the right hypothesis for
gluing families. The computation rules `glue_apply`, `glue_eq_left_of_some` and
`glue_eq_right_of_none` pin down the value of a glue case by case, and
`support_glue_eq_union` shows that gluing unions the domains:
`Support (glue f g) = Support f ∪ Support g`.

## 3. The binary gluing theorem

The heart of the development consists of four results.

* `glue_extends_left : glue f g ⊒ f`. The glue always extends its first
  argument, with no hypothesis: where `f` has a value, the glue keeps it.

* `glue_extends_right : Compatible f g → glue f g ⊒ g`. The glue extends its
  second argument *exactly when* the two sections are compatible. If `g` records
  `a` at `i` while `f` records a different `b`, the glue would return `b` and
  fail to extend `g`; compatibility rules this out.

* `glue_unique : h ⊒ f → h ⊒ g → Support h ⊆ Support f ∪ Support g → h =
  glue f g`. Any common extension that introduces no spurious data beyond the
  combined support *is* the glue. Thus the glue is the unique minimal common
  extension.

* `compatible_of_common_extension : h ⊒ f → h ⊒ g → Compatible f g`. If a common
  extension exists at all, the sections must have been compatible: `h` cannot
  simultaneously equal two different values at one index.

Together with `support_glue_eq_union`, these assemble into the central
equivalence

```
compatible_iff_exists_common_extension :
  Compatible f g ↔ ∃ h, h ⊒ f ∧ h ⊒ g ∧ Support h ⊆ Support f ∪ Support g.
```

This is the gluing axiom of a sheaf in its cleanest form: *local data can be
amalgamated into a global section if and only if it is pairwise consistent on
overlaps.* The forward direction constructs the glue; the backward direction
recovers compatibility from the mere existence of an amalgamation.

## 4. Locality (separation)

The second sheaf axiom — that a section is determined by its restrictions to a
cover — appears as

```
restrict_locality :
  (∀ i, ∃ j, i ∈ U j) → (∀ j, restrict f (U j) = restrict g (U j)) → f = g.
```

If the sets `U j` cover the index set and `f` and `g` agree after restriction to
every `U j`, then `f = g` everywhere. The proof is pointwise: each index `i`
lies in some `U j`, on which the restrictions coincide, forcing `f i = g i`.
This is the *separation* (or *monopresheaf*) condition; combined with Section 3
it makes `PartialSection` a genuine sheaf of data on the discrete index set.

## 5. Gluing arbitrary families

For an indexed family `s : β → PartialSection ι α` we define
`PairwiseCompatible s := ∀ b c, Compatible (s b) (s c)` and the amalgamation

```
familyGlue s i :=
  if some member of the family has a value at i then (a choice of such a value)
  else none.
```

`familyGlue` is `noncomputable`, using `Classical.choice` only to select, at
each index, one of the values offered by the family. The selection is harmless
precisely because of pairwise compatibility: all offered values coincide. We
prove

* `familyGlue_extends : PairwiseCompatible s → ∀ b, familyGlue s ⊒ s b`, and
* `glue_family_exists : PairwiseCompatible s → ∃ h, ∀ b, h ⊒ s b`.

Thus an arbitrarily large consistent collection of partial records can always be
merged into a single record that faithfully extends every member, generalising
the binary gluing theorem to families of any cardinality.

## 6. Why this formalizes sheaf-style data integration with missing values

In applications, a "global object" (a complete record, a full configuration, a
reconciled data set) is rarely observed directly. Instead one observes many
*partial* views, each missing some fields: different sensors report different
coordinates, different sources fill different columns, different surveys answer
different questions. The questions are then:

1. **Consistency.** When can these partial views possibly come from one global
   object? Answer: exactly when they are pairwise compatible — they never
   disagree on a shared field. This is `compatible_iff_exists_common_extension`
   and `PairwiseCompatible`.

2. **Integration.** Given consistency, how do we build the integrated record?
   Answer: glue them — `glue` for two, `familyGlue` for many — which is well
   defined and extends every input (`glue_extends_left/right`,
   `familyGlue_extends`).

3. **Uniqueness / no fabrication.** Does integration invent information? Answer:
   no — the glue is the unique common extension with support contained in the
   union of inputs (`glue_unique`), so it adds nothing that was not present in
   some source.

4. **Locality.** Is the integrated record pinned down by what we can see on
   each part of a cover? Answer: yes (`restrict_locality`), so the global
   reconstruction is unambiguous.

These are precisely the sheaf axioms — *gluing* and *separation* — read as a
theory of data integration. The use of `Option` to model missing values, rather
than partial functions or subtypes, keeps every construction first-order and
decidable in structure (only the family-level choice is noncomputable), making
the entire development elementary and machine-checked end to end.

This file develops the *deterministic algebraic skeleton* underlying the
random-matrix phenomenology of large weight matrices (e.g. the singular-value
spectra of transformer / LLM weight matrices, which empirically follow
Marchenko–Pastur (MP) statistics with a small number of detached "spike"
singular values).

We work entirely with the **deterministic limiting objects** of random matrix
theory, where every statement is an exact real-analytic identity or inequality.
This isolates the genuinely provable mathematical content of the universality
story — the location of the bulk, the closing of the spectral gap, and the
BBP (Baik–Ben Arous–Péché) spike transition — from the probabilistic limit
theorems (semicircle / MP law) that are out of reach of the current library.

## The model

For a rectangular weight matrix `W` of shape `M × N` with i.i.d.-scaled entries,
the eigenvalues of the Gram matrix `(1/N) WᵀW` fill, as `M, N → ∞` with aspect
ratio `λ = M/N` fixed, the Marchenko–Pastur sea supported on `[e₋, e₊]` with

  `e₋(λ) = (1 - √λ)²`,   `e₊(λ) = (1 + √λ)²`.

A rank-one "spike" of strength `ℓ > 1` planted in the population covariance
produces a single detached eigenvalue at

  `outlier(ℓ, λ) = ℓ + λ·ℓ/(ℓ - 1)`

once `ℓ` exceeds the **BBP threshold** `ℓ_c(λ) = 1 + √λ`.

## Main results

* `bulkWidth` : the bulk has width `e₊ - e₋ = 4√λ`.
* `edge_sum`, `edge_prod` : `e₋ + e₊ = 2(1+λ)`, `e₋·e₊ = (1-λ)²`.
* `edgeMinus_pos` / `edgeMinus_eq_zero_iff` : the **hard-gap phase transition** —
  the lower edge is strictly positive for `λ < 1` and collapses to `0` exactly
  at `λ = 1` (the square / invertibility boundary for weight matrices).
* `outlier_sub_edgePlus` : the *exact* secular identity
  `outlier(ℓ,λ) - e₊(λ) = ((ℓ-1) - √λ)² / (ℓ-1)`.
* `outlier_ge_edgePlus`, `outlier_at_threshold` : the outlier never enters the
  bulk and touches the edge exactly at the BBP threshold.
* `outlier_strictMono_supercrit` / `outlier_strictAnti_subcrit` : the **BBP
  phase transition** as a monotonicity reversal of the spike map at `ℓ = ℓ_c`.
* `outlier_min_at_threshold` : the threshold is the unique minimizer of the
  spike map, with minimum value the bulk edge.

import Mathlib

open Real

namespace SpectralUniversality

/-! ## Marchenko–Pastur bulk edges -/

/-- Lower edge of the Marchenko–Pastur sea at aspect ratio `lam = M/N`. -/
noncomputable def edgeMinus (lam : ℝ) : ℝ := (1 - Real.sqrt lam) ^ 2

/-- Upper edge of the Marchenko–Pastur sea at aspect ratio `lam = M/N`. -/
noncomputable def edgePlus (lam : ℝ) : ℝ := (1 + Real.sqrt lam) ^ 2

theorem edgeMinus_nonneg (lam : ℝ) : 0 ≤ edgeMinus lam := sq_nonneg _

theorem edgePlus_nonneg (lam : ℝ) : 0 ≤ edgePlus lam := sq_nonneg _

/-- The lower edge never exceeds the upper edge. -/
theorem edgeMinus_le_edgePlus (lam : ℝ) : edgeMinus lam ≤ edgePlus lam := by
  unfold edgeMinus edgePlus
  nlinarith [Real.sqrt_nonneg lam]

/-- The spectral bulk has width `4√λ`. -/
theorem bulkWidth (lam : ℝ) : edgePlus lam - edgeMinus lam = 4 * Real.sqrt lam := by
  unfold edgePlus edgeMinus; ring

/-- First symmetric function of the edges: `e₋ + e₊ = 2(1 + λ)`. -/
theorem edge_sum (lam : ℝ) (h : 0 ≤ lam) : edgeMinus lam + edgePlus lam = 2 * (1 + lam) := by
  unfold edgeMinus edgePlus
  nlinarith [Real.sq_sqrt h]

/-- Second symmetric function of the edges: `e₋ · e₊ = (1 - λ)²`. -/
theorem edge_prod (lam : ℝ) (h : 0 ≤ lam) : edgeMinus lam * edgePlus lam = (1 - lam) ^ 2 := by
  unfold edgeMinus edgePlus
  nlinarith [Real.sq_sqrt h]

/-- **Hard-gap phase, subcritical side.** For `λ < 1` the bulk stays strictly
away from `0`: the Gram matrix has a hard spectral gap (and the rectangular
weight matrix is well-conditioned / full rank in the limit). -/
theorem edgeMinus_pos (lam : ℝ) (h0 : 0 ≤ lam) (h1 : lam < 1) : 0 < edgeMinus lam := by
  unfold edgeMinus
  have hs : Real.sqrt lam < 1 := by
    rw [show (1 : ℝ) = Real.sqrt 1 by simp]
    exact Real.sqrt_lt_sqrt h0 h1
  have : (0 : ℝ) < 1 - Real.sqrt lam := by linarith
  positivity

/-- **Gap-closing phase transition.** The lower edge collapses to `0` *exactly*
at the square aspect ratio `λ = 1`. -/
theorem edgeMinus_eq_zero_iff (lam : ℝ) (h : 0 ≤ lam) : edgeMinus lam = 0 ↔ lam = 1 := by
  unfold edgeMinus
  rw [pow_eq_zero_iff (by norm_num)]
  constructor
  · intro hh
    have : Real.sqrt lam = 1 := by linarith
    nlinarith [Real.sq_sqrt h, this]
  · intro hh; subst hh; simp

/-! ## BBP spike transition -/

/-- The BBP critical spike strength `ℓ_c(λ) = 1 + √λ`. -/
noncomputable def bbpThreshold (lam : ℝ) : ℝ := 1 + Real.sqrt lam

/-- Deterministic location of the detached eigenvalue produced by a population
spike of strength `ℓ` at aspect ratio `λ`. -/
noncomputable def outlier (ell lam : ℝ) : ℝ := ell + lam * ell / (ell - 1)

/-- **The secular identity.** The signed distance of the outlier from the upper
bulk edge is a perfect square divided by `ℓ - 1`. This single identity drives
every BBP statement below. -/
theorem outlier_sub_edgePlus (lam ell : ℝ) (h : 0 ≤ lam) (hl : 1 < ell) :
    outlier ell lam - edgePlus lam = ((ell - 1) - Real.sqrt lam) ^ 2 / (ell - 1) := by
  unfold outlier edgePlus
  have ht : ell - 1 ≠ 0 := by linarith
  field_simp
  nlinarith [Real.sq_sqrt h]

/-- The outlier never enters the bulk: `outlier(ℓ,λ) ≥ e₊(λ)` for all `ℓ > 1`. -/
theorem outlier_ge_edgePlus (lam ell : ℝ) (h : 0 ≤ lam) (hl : 1 < ell) :
    edgePlus lam ≤ outlier ell lam := by
  have key := outlier_sub_edgePlus lam ell h hl
  have hpos : 0 ≤ ((ell - 1) - Real.sqrt lam) ^ 2 / (ell - 1) :=
    div_nonneg (sq_nonneg _) (by linarith)
  linarith

/-- At the BBP threshold the outlier is exactly tangent to the bulk edge. -/
theorem outlier_at_threshold (lam : ℝ) (h : 0 < lam) :
    outlier (bbpThreshold lam) lam = edgePlus lam := by
  have hl : 1 < bbpThreshold lam := by
    unfold bbpThreshold; have := Real.sqrt_pos.mpr h; linarith
  have key := outlier_sub_edgePlus lam (bbpThreshold lam) h.le hl
  unfold bbpThreshold at key
  simp only [add_sub_cancel_left] at key
  norm_num at key
  unfold bbpThreshold; linarith

/-- **BBP transition, supercritical branch.** Above the threshold the spike map
is strictly increasing: a stronger planted spike pushes the detached eigenvalue
strictly further from the bulk. -/
theorem outlier_strictMono_supercrit (lam a b : ℝ) (h : 0 < lam)
    (ha : bbpThreshold lam ≤ a) (hab : a < b) : outlier a lam < outlier b lam := by
  have hsq := Real.sq_sqrt h.le
  have hs := Real.sqrt_pos.mpr h
  have ha1 : Real.sqrt lam ≤ a - 1 := by unfold bbpThreshold at ha; linarith
  have hb1 : Real.sqrt lam < b - 1 := by unfold bbpThreshold at ha; linarith
  have hap : 0 < a - 1 := by linarith
  have hbp : 0 < b - 1 := by linarith
  have hprod : lam < (a - 1) * (b - 1) := by nlinarith [hsq]
  have expand : outlier b lam - outlier a lam = (b - a) * (1 - lam / ((a - 1) * (b - 1))) := by
    unfold outlier; field_simp; ring
  have hfac : 0 < 1 - lam / ((a - 1) * (b - 1)) := by
    have : lam / ((a - 1) * (b - 1)) < 1 := by rw [div_lt_one (by positivity)]; exact hprod
    linarith
  nlinarith [expand, hfac, hab]

/-- **BBP transition, subcritical branch.** Below the threshold the spike map is
strictly *decreasing*: this is the spurious (non-physical) root, absorbed into
the bulk. The reversal of monotonicity at `ℓ_c` is the phase transition. -/
theorem outlier_strictAnti_subcrit (lam a b : ℝ) (h : 0 < lam)
    (ha : 1 < a) (hab : a < b) (hb : b ≤ bbpThreshold lam) : outlier b lam < outlier a lam := by
  have hsq := Real.sq_sqrt h.le
  have ha1 : a - 1 < Real.sqrt lam := by unfold bbpThreshold at hb; linarith
  have hb1 : b - 1 ≤ Real.sqrt lam := by unfold bbpThreshold at hb; linarith
  have hap : 0 < a - 1 := by linarith
  have hbp : 0 < b - 1 := by linarith
  have hprod : (a - 1) * (b - 1) < lam := by nlinarith [hsq]
  have expand : outlier b lam - outlier a lam = (b - a) * (1 - lam / ((a - 1) * (b - 1))) := by
    unfold outlier; field_simp; ring
  have hfac : 1 - lam / ((a - 1) * (b - 1)) < 0 := by
    have : 1 < lam / ((a - 1) * (b - 1)) := by
      rw [lt_div_iff₀ (by positivity)]; nlinarith [hprod]
    linarith
  nlinarith [expand, hfac, hab]

/-- **Synthesis: the BBP threshold is the unique minimizer of the spike map** on
`(1, ∞)`, with minimum value the bulk edge `e₊`. This packages the gap, the
secular identity, and the monotonicity reversal into one statement. -/
theorem outlier_min_at_threshold (lam ell : ℝ) (h : 0 < lam) (hl : 1 < ell)
    (hne : ell ≠ bbpThreshold lam) : edgePlus lam < outlier ell lam := by
  have key := outlier_sub_edgePlus lam ell h.le hl
  have hne0 : (ell - 1) - Real.sqrt lam ≠ 0 := by
    intro hz; apply hne; unfold bbpThreshold; linarith
  have hpos : 0 < ((ell - 1) - Real.sqrt lam) ^ 2 / (ell - 1) := by
    apply div_pos _ (by linarith)
    exact lt_of_le_of_ne (sq_nonneg _) (Ne.symm (pow_ne_zero 2 hne0))
  linarith

end SpectralUniversality

import Mathlib

open Real

namespace SpectralUniversality

/-! ## Additive (Wigner / GOE) BBP transition -/

/-- Location of the detached eigenvalue of a rank-one additive perturbation of
strength `theta` of a Wigner bulk supported on `[-2, 2]`. -/
noncomputable def wignerOutlier (theta : ℝ) : ℝ := theta + 1 / theta

/-- Exact secular identity for the additive model: distance from the bulk edge
`2` is a perfect square over `theta`. -/
theorem wignerOutlier_sub_two (theta : ℝ) (h : 0 < theta) :
    wignerOutlier theta - 2 = (theta - 1) ^ 2 / theta := by
  unfold wignerOutlier; field_simp; ring

/-- The additive outlier never enters the bulk: `θ + 1/θ ≥ 2`. -/
theorem wignerOutlier_ge_two (theta : ℝ) (h : 0 < theta) : 2 ≤ wignerOutlier theta := by
  have h1 : 0 ≤ (theta - 1) ^ 2 / theta := div_nonneg (sq_nonneg _) h.le
  nlinarith [wignerOutlier_sub_two theta h, h1]

/-- **Additive BBP, supercritical branch.** Strictly increasing for `θ ≥ 1`. -/
theorem wignerOutlier_mono (a b : ℝ) (ha : 1 ≤ a) (hab : a < b) :
    wignerOutlier a < wignerOutlier b := by
  have ha0 : 0 < a := by linarith
  have hb : 0 < b := by linarith
  have expand : wignerOutlier b - wignerOutlier a = (b - a) * (1 - 1 / (a * b)) := by
    unfold wignerOutlier; field_simp; ring
  have hfac : 0 < 1 - 1 / (a * b) := by
    have : 1 / (a * b) < 1 := by rw [div_lt_one (by positivity)]; nlinarith
    linarith
  nlinarith [expand, hfac]

/-- **Additive BBP, subcritical branch.** Strictly decreasing for `0 < θ ≤ 1`:
the spurious root absorbed into the bulk. Reversal at `θ = 1` is the transition. -/
theorem wignerOutlier_anti (a b : ℝ) (ha : 0 < a) (hab : a < b) (hb : b ≤ 1) :
    wignerOutlier b < wignerOutlier a := by
  have hb0 : 0 < b := by linarith
  have expand : wignerOutlier b - wignerOutlier a = (b - a) * (1 - 1 / (a * b)) := by
    unfold wignerOutlier; field_simp; ring
  have hfac : 1 - 1 / (a * b) < 0 := by
    have : 1 < 1 / (a * b) := by rw [lt_div_iff₀ (by positivity)]; nlinarith
    linarith
  nlinarith [expand, hfac]

/-! ## Eigenvector alignment / signal-recovery transition (multiplicative model) -/

/-- Squared overlap between the sample top eigenvector and the planted spike
direction in the Marchenko–Pastur spiked model. -/
noncomputable def overlap (ell lam : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (1 - lam / (ell - 1) ^ 2) / (1 + lam / (ell - 1))

/-- **Recovery transition.** The alignment vanishes *exactly* at the BBP
threshold `ℓ_c = 1 + √λ` — the same critical point as eigenvalue detachment. -/
theorem overlap_at_threshold (lam : ℝ) (h : 0 < lam) :
    overlap (1 + Real.sqrt lam) lam = 0 := by
  unfold overlap
  have hsq := Real.sq_sqrt h.le
  have hlam : lam ≠ 0 := ne_of_gt h
  have he : (1 + Real.sqrt lam) - 1 = Real.sqrt lam := by ring
  rw [div_eq_zero_iff]; left
  rw [he, hsq, div_self hlam]; ring

/-- Above the threshold the alignment is strictly positive: nontrivial recovery
of the planted signal. -/
theorem overlap_pos_supercrit (lam ell : ℝ) (h : 0 < lam) (hl : 1 < ell)
    (hsuper : 1 + Real.sqrt lam < ell) : 0 < overlap ell lam := by
  unfold overlap
  have hsq := Real.sq_sqrt h.le
  have ht : 0 < ell - 1 := by linarith
  have hnum : 0 < 1 - lam / (ell - 1) ^ 2 := by
    have : lam / (ell - 1) ^ 2 < 1 := by
      rw [div_lt_one (by positivity)]
      have : Real.sqrt lam < ell - 1 := by linarith
      nlinarith [hsq, Real.sqrt_nonneg lam]
    linarith
  have hden : 0 < 1 + lam / (ell - 1) := by positivity
  exact div_pos hnum hden

/-- Below the threshold the alignment *formula* is negative — there is no
recovery (the physical overlap is clipped to `0`). -/
theorem overlap_neg_subcrit (lam ell : ℝ) (h : 0 < lam) (hl : 1 < ell)
    (hsub : ell < 1 + Real.sqrt lam) : overlap ell lam < 0 := by
  unfold overlap
  have hsq := Real.sq_sqrt h.le
  have ht : 0 < ell - 1 := by linarith
  have hnum : 1 - lam / (ell - 1) ^ 2 < 0 := by
    have : 1 < lam / (ell - 1) ^ 2 := by
      rw [lt_div_iff₀ (by positivity)]
      have : ell - 1 < Real.sqrt lam := by linarith
      nlinarith [hsq, Real.sqrt_nonneg lam]
    linarith
  have hden : 0 < 1 + lam / (ell - 1) := by positivity
  exact div_neg_of_neg_of_pos hnum hden

/-- Alignment is never perfect at finite spike strength: `overlap < 1`. -/
theorem overlap_lt_one (lam ell : ℝ) (h : 0 < lam) (hl : 1 < ell) : overlap ell lam < 1 := by
  unfold overlap
  have ht : 0 < ell - 1 := by linarith
  have hden : 0 < 1 + lam / (ell - 1) := by positivity
  rw [div_lt_one hden]
  have h1 : 0 < lam / (ell - 1) := by positivity
  have h2 : 0 ≤ lam / (ell - 1) ^ 2 := by positivity
  linarith

end SpectralUniversality
